summary.text: For consecutive divisors \(d<e\) of \(n\), a gap \(e>2d\) forces \(e\) to be odd: if \(e\) were even, then \(e/2\) would be another divisor strictly between \(d\) and \(e\); conversely, oddness together with \(e\ge 2d\) rules out equality and hence gives \(e>2d\). Thus the formula counting one plus the adjacent pairs with odd upper divisor and \(e\ge2d\) equals one plus the number of gaps, which is exactly the number of maximal blocks.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
D(n)=(d_1,d_2,\ldots,d_m)
\]
be the divisors of the positive integer \(n\), listed in strictly increasing order. Thus \(m\geq 1\), since \(1\mid n\).

We use the stated characterization of A237271:
\[
a(n)=1+\#\bigl\{i:1\leq i<m,\ d_{i+1}\text{ is odd and }d_{i+1}\geq 2d_i\bigr\}.
\tag{1}
\]
We will prove that the set counted on the right of (1) is exactly the set of breaks between the maximal contiguous sublists of \(D(n)\) in which each term is at most twice its predecessor.

The essential fact is the following lemma.

**Lemma.** If \(a<b\) are consecutive divisors of \(n\), then
\[
b>2a \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b\text{ is odd and }b\geq 2a.
\tag{2}
\]

**Proof of the lemma.** Because \(a\) and \(b\) are consecutive in the increasing list of divisors, every divisor \(z\) of \(n\) satisfying \(z<b\) must satisfy \(z\leq a\). Indeed, otherwise \(a<z<b\) would be a divisor strictly between two consecutive divisors.

First suppose that \(b>2a\). We claim that \(b\) is odd. If instead \(b\) were even, write \(b=2k\). Since \(k\mid b\) and \(b\mid n\), transitivity of divisibility gives \(k\mid n\). Also \(b>0\), and hence \(k<b\). The consecutiveness property just established would then imply \(k\leq a\). Consequently
\[
b=2k\leq 2a,
\]
contradicting \(b>2a\). Thus \(b\) is odd. Of course \(b>2a\) also implies \(b\geq 2a\), proving the forward implication in (2).

Conversely, suppose that \(b\) is odd and \(b\geq 2a\). Equality \(b=2a\) is impossible, because \(2a\) is even whereas \(b\) is odd. Therefore the inequality must be strict: \(b>2a\). This proves the reverse implication and hence the lemma. \(\square\)

We now identify the maximal \(2\)-dense sublists. For each adjacent pair \((d_i,d_{i+1})\), call the position between them a **break** if
\[
d_{i+1}>2d_i.
\tag{3}
\]
Cut the increasing divisor list at every such position. This partitions \(D(n)\) into contiguous, nonempty blocks.

Within any one of these blocks, no adjacent position is a break. Therefore every adjacent pair in the block satisfies
\[
d_{i+1}\leq 2d_i.
\]
Thus each block is a \(2\)-dense contiguous sublist in the sense of the conjecture.

Each block is also maximal. If a block has a divisor immediately before it, then the block begins just after a break, so adjoining that preceding divisor would introduce an adjacent pair with \(d_{i+1}>2d_i\). Likewise, if a block has a divisor immediately after it, then the block ends just before a break, and adjoining the following divisor would violate the same condition. Hence no block can be enlarged to a larger contiguous \(2\)-dense sublist.

Conversely, every maximal contiguous \(2\)-dense sublist must be one of these blocks. It cannot cross a break, since at a break the next divisor is greater than twice the preceding one. And if it were a proper contiguous sublist of one of the blocks, it could be extended by the neighboring divisor within that block while preserving all adjacent inequalities, contradicting maximality. Therefore the blocks obtained by cutting at (3) are exactly all the maximal \(2\)-dense sublists.

Since \(D(n)\) is nonempty, cutting a list at \(r\) positions produces exactly \(r+1\) nonempty blocks. It follows that the number of maximal \(2\)-dense sublists is
\[
1+\#\bigl\{i:1\leq i<m,\ d_{i+1}>2d_i\bigr\}.
\tag{4}
\]

Finally, apply the lemma to every consecutive pair \(d_i<d_{i+1}\). It gives, for each index \(i\),
\[
d_{i+1}>2d_i
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\bigl(d_{i+1}\text{ is odd and }d_{i+1}\geq 2d_i\bigr).
\]
Thus the set of indices counted in (4) is exactly the set of indices counted in (1). Their cardinalities are equal, and hence
\[
\#\{\text{maximal \(2\)-dense contiguous sublists of divisors of }n\}
=1+\#\bigl\{i:d_{i+1}\text{ odd},\ d_{i+1}\geq2d_i\bigr\}
=a(n).
\]

This also covers \(n=1\): its divisor list is \((1)\), there are no adjacent pairs or breaks, and there is exactly one maximal block. Therefore the claimed equality holds for every \(n\geq1\).
